items.title: PLAUSIBLY EXPLAINED (2026-09-13): a real transient production 502/timeout was observed during independent QA, self-recovered; a matching real mechanism was later found and fixed
items.scope: agentic-platform-backend Railway service (production)
items.reason: The native qa-evaluator subagent, while independently verifying Phase 1+2 against production (2026-09-11), observed a real HTTP 502 Bad Gateway from Railway's own edge on /learn after a ~300s hang, followed by several minutes of request timeouts, with general internet connectivity confirmed fine throughout. Production self-recovered; an immediate rerun of curl, the Python suite, and the full Playwright suite all passed cleanly. Root cause NOT established -- plausibly an unrelated Railway platform event, OR the burst of ~13 concurrent Playwright browser sessions (used for this task's own verification) straining the backend. This is evidence worth the Owner's attention, not a contract failure (uptime/resilience under concurrent E2E load was not one of the stated acceptance criteria) and NOT something this autonomous task should decide how to address (could imply needing Railway plan changes, backend concurrency limits, or simply monitoring -- all business/infrastructure judgment calls).
items.evidence: qa-evaluator's own verification report (2026-09-11, task 'Independent QA of Phase 1+2 fixes') -- observed via direct curl against the real production edge, includes response headers (server: railway-hikari, x-railway-edge: ams1). UPDATE (2026-09-13, WORKBENCH RELIABILITY session): a real, independently-confirmed full-service outage on the SAME platform-backend service was root-caused this task via a direct pg_stat_activity query -- a connection left idle-in-transaction for 963s, holding a lock that blocked ensure_schema()'s DDL, which nearly every request-serving code path calls first; compounded by 4 route handlers running real synchronous DB queries directly on the asyncio event loop, so one stuck query froze every concurrent request. Fixed (commit 4e15656): run_in_threadpool for all 4 handlers, a 15s statement_timeout, and a 30s idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on every event-ledger connection. This is a PLAUSIBLE, not certain, explanation for the 2026-09-11 event specifically (the exact failing query/connection from that date was never captured) -- offered as the most consistent known mechanism, not claimed as definitively proven for that specific historical incident.
items.verification_required: Owner decision, narrowed by the 2026-09-13 fix: with the event loop no longer blockable by one slow DB call and Postgres now self-terminating orphaned idle-in-transaction connections, decide whether the remaining residual risk (e.g. bounding Playwright's local worker concurrency against production, or upgrading the event-ledger Postgres plan) still needs action, or whether this class of failure is now adequately mitigated.

items.title: NEEDS_OWNER_DECISION (narrowed): secure git-push architecture now implemented and proven live end-to-end; only the write-credential itself remains an explicit Owner decision
items.scope: agent/demo_execution.py (create_isolated_workspace/commit_change/push_change/trigger_deploy/wait_for_new_deployment), agent/web_server.py's _run_trainer_thread/_run_reset_thread
items.reason: WORKBENCH RELIABILITY P0 (2026-09-13) redesigned this from scratch after determining the deployed container's own long-lived checkout was never the right thing to mutate/push at all (the original question this action item asked before any fix: 'is this environment supposed to mutate/push a Git checkout, or should it use an isolated workspace instead?' -- answer: isolated workspace). Each run now clones a fresh, disposable temp-dir workspace from the real public GitHub URL (never touches the container's own long-lived checkout), commits to a dedicated `demo/<run_id>` branch (never master), and pushes only if `DEMO_GIT_PUSH_TOKEN` is configured (still NOT provisioned -- an explicit Owner secret decision this task still does not make unilaterally); an unconfigured token is treated as an honest no-op, never a silent failure, and the token is redacted from all captured subprocess output before it can reach any logged/streamed event. `railway link`/`railway up` were separately hardened as non-fatal-link-then-deploy-anyway (see the 4 real production incidents root-caused this same phase, recorded in docs/LESSONS.md), and deployment identity is now proven via real Railway metadata timestamps rather than id-difference guessing. A real end-to-end acceptance run (Playwright, RUN_REAL_ACCEPTANCE=1) exercising the full isolated-workspace -> commit -> push-attempt -> deploy -> timestamp-verified-new-deployment -> production-content-verified -> reset chain passed against live production (2026-09-13), independently re-confirmed via direct curl.

items.title: RESOLVED IN FOUNDATION (2026-09-13): the backend production-verification mechanism now exists and was proven live end-to-end -- still INTERNAL/GATED, not publicly enabled
items.scope: agent/backend_catalogue.py, agent/backend_execution.py, agent/backend_acceptance.py (new, internal-only -- no public Workbench route touches any of this)
items.reason: The structural gap this item originally identified (no verification mechanism exists that can derive a targeted, deterministic production assertion from a compiled Java/Spring change) is now CLOSED at the foundation level, mirroring demo_catalogue.py's anchor-pattern design applied to one Java string constant (CustomerService.CUSTOMER_NOT_FOUND_MESSAGE, deliberately isolated for exactly this purpose in a separate commit this same phase) instead of static HTML, with a JSON-field extractor (backend_catalogue.extract_value_from_not_found_api_response) instead of a DOM/text anchor. A REAL, LIVE, end-to-end internal acceptance run (agent/backend_acceptance.py) was executed against real production this phase, using a safe, clearly-marked test value, never the actual reserved future target text ('Customer record not found'): real isolated-workspace clone from the real public GitHub repo -> real `mvnw compile` -> real targeted JUnit + the real RestTemplate-based integration test -> real git commit (dedicated branch, never master) -> real git push attempt (honestly NOT_CONFIGURED, ACT-007) -> real Railway deploy -> real deployment-identity confirmation (timestamp-parsed, not raw-string-compared) -> a real live GET /customers/<id> API call independently confirming the exact probe value live in production -> a second full cycle restoring the real baseline, independently reconfirmed live. Three genuine, previously-unknown production-blocking defects were found and fixed getting here (see docs/LESSONS.md and the 3 commits fixing them): app/mvnw was never git-tracked as executable (100644, not 100755); this machine's core.autocrlf=true corrupted app/mvnw's shebang to CRLF on every fresh clone (fixed via .gitattributes, the durable fix -- not a per-machine workaround); and wait_for_new_deployment() compared deployment timestamps as raw strings instead of parsed datetimes, which happened to work for every prior fixture but is not reliably correct in general (fixed, with a constructed counterexample regression test). One honest, not-yet-explained limitation: the acceptance script's own end-to-end run experienced an unexplained polling delay after Railway genuinely reached SUCCESS status (production was independently confirmed correct via direct curl and via a direct, isolated call to the same wait_for_new_deployment() function, which found the real deployment correctly in 10s) -- worth a future investigation, not blocking, and not hidden.

items.reason: The Owner's 'MASTER BUILD PHASE' session explicitly pre-approved exactly one new persistent resource: a dedicated Postgres for the Customer App, separate from the event-ledger Postgres. Provisioned via `railway add --database postgres` in the agentic-delivery-customer-app project (no billing/upgrade prompt appeared). Wired the customer-app service to it via DATABASE_URL/DATABASE_USERNAME/DATABASE_PASSWORD referencing the new Postgres service's variables (Railway private-network hostname, `${{Postgres.PGHOST}}` etc.) plus SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=postgres.
items.evidence: REAL PRODUCTION-CUTOVER FINDING (not hypothetical): the first redeploy (env-var change only) reused Railway's existing built image without a rebuild -- logs showed profile 'postgres' active but the datasource was STILL jdbc:h2:mem and only 1 of 3 JPA repositories was found, proving the deployed image predated the Postgres/Preference/ContractPlan code entirely (the customer-app service does not auto-deploy on git push -- see docs/LESSONS.md). Fixed by running `railway up -s agentic-delivery-customer-app` from app/ to force a real rebuild from current source (new image digest 39c5675982d7). Deploy logs from the real rebuild show: 3 JPA repositories found, Flyway connected to `jdbc:postgresql://postgres.railway.internal:5432/railway` (PostgreSQL 18.6), schema history table created from `<< Empty Schema >>`, and V1/V2/V3 migrations applied in order ('Successfully applied 3 migrations ... now at version v3'). Live API smoke test against production: POST /customers (201, real row), GET /customers/{id}, GET /customers/{id}/preferences (default-created), POST + GET /customers/{id}/plan (enroll + read-active) all returned correct real data. Persistence-survives-restart verified: `railway redeploy` (same image, no rebuild) followed by re-curling the same customer/plan confirmed the exact same data was still present.
items.verification_required: DONE: Flyway-from-empty-DB, startup/health, and a full create/read/enroll API cycle were all independently verified against real production, not simulated. NOT YET DONE, intentionally out of this action's scope: DB-level partial-unique-index business-rule verification against the NEW production Postgres specifically (already proven against a Testcontainers Postgres in CI, not re-proven here); H2 profile files were left in place (not deleted) as a documented local-dev fallback.

items.title: RESOLVED (2026-09-14): real root cause was a display-truncation cap silently limiting RAG indexing past 200 files, not just test isolation
items.scope: agent/tools.py (list_repository_files refactored into a shared _walk_repository_files helper + new list_all_repository_files for exhaustive internal callers), agent/rag_index.py (_indexable_files now uses list_all_repository_files), agent/test_rag_index.py (one assertion corrected)
items.reason: PORTFOLIO COMPLETION PUSH session, Phase -1/Priority 1: root-caused rather than worked around per this task's own 'find root cause' instruction. The real defect was NOT test isolation alone -- agent/rag_index.py's _indexable_files() reused tools.list_repository_files(), which intentionally truncates to MAX_FILES_LISTED=200 (alphabetically sorted) for the LLM agent's token budget. The repository genuinely grew past 200 indexable files, so the whole-repo RAG index was silently missing every file sorted after position 200 -- a real, live gap in the actual index (used by the offline V3 CLI agent), not merely a fixture-ordering coincidence. Fixed by factoring the untruncated directory walk into tools._walk_repository_files() and exposing it via a new tools.list_all_repository_files() (not an LLM-facing tool) for exhaustive internal callers; list_repository_files()'s existing truncated contract for the LLM agent is completely unchanged. A 5th failure (test_env_and_git_and_target_never_indexable) was a separate, unrelated test bug: a bare '.git' substring check false-matched the legitimately-indexable .github/workflows/ci.yml -- corrected to check for the real .git directory path segment. See docs/LESSONS.md for both generalized lessons.
items.evidence: python agent/test_rag_index.py -v: 13/13 pass (previously 5/13 failed). Full python -m unittest discover -p 'test_*.py' from agent/: Ran 531 tests in 297.188s, OK (skipped=1) -- 0 failures, genuinely clean baseline. Node (23+36+33=92/92 passing) and Java (mvnw test, BUILD SUCCESS) independently re-confirmed unaffected by this Python-only change.

items.title: ENVIRONMENT_LIMITATION (Owner-classified, not a product defect): local machine memory pressure killed the full Python regression suite twice during the flagship-completion session's Checkpoint 3
items.scope: This dev machine's own available RAM only -- no code change, no test change needed to resolve this specific item.
items.reason: During Checkpoint 3 (Triage Scenario C + a shared-engine reliability fix), `python -m unittest discover -p 'test_*.py'` (the full ~600-test suite) was killed twice by the OS due to low system memory (observed ~2.3GB free of ~16GB total, likely from many hours of accumulated Maven/Node/browser-automation/IDE processes across this long session). This is a real, observed local resource constraint -- not a test failure, and not evidence of a code regression. The Owner explicitly instructed: stop retrying the same memory-heavy full suite locally, run only targeted tests for the actual change, and treat GitHub Actions CI as the authoritative full-suite lane. Checkpoint 3's changes were verified instead via: the complete agent/test_triage_execution.py suite (47/47, covering every function touched), the specific Java Scenario C test classes (TriageScenarioCIntegrationTest 4/4, TriageScenarioCPostgresIntegrationTest 2/2 honestly skipped -- no local Docker), and direct live-production verification of the actual deployed behavior (curl-level end-to-end Scenario C lifecycle, including the reliability-fixed candidate-patch step).
items.evidence: Two killed background task runs during this session (memory pressure, not test assertions failing) -- see docs/PROJECT_STATE.json's CHECKPOINT 3 completed_capabilities entry for the full narrative. A lingering ~3.16GB python.exe process from one of the killed runs was found and terminated (taskkill) before targeted verification proceeded.
